opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is one of the most underappreciated dynamics in thinking about long-run trajectories, including for AI.

The basic idea is that we often imagine history as a story of choices: leaders decide things, cultures adopt values, societies pick institutions. And those choices do matter. But over longer time horizons, there's a selection process operating on top of them. Civilisations, states, firms, and institutions that are better at generating economic surplus and converting it into military power tend to persist and spread, while those that aren't tend to be absorbed, conquered, outcompeted, or forced to imitate. So the menu of options any individual society actually has is constrained by what its competitors are doing.

You can see this in the history of technology adoption. Japan in the 1850s and 60s didn't really get to choose whether to industrialise in some unconstrained way. The arrival of Western gunboats made it clear that societies which didn't adopt industrial and military technologies were going to lose autonomy. The Meiji reformers made a choice, but it was a choice made under intense structural pressure. The same goes for the spread of the bureaucratic state, mass conscription, and gunpowder before that. Societies that held out often didn't survive as independent political units.

So I'd describe it as a kind of filter. Individual actors make decisions, but the competitive environment determines which decisions get rewarded with survival and influence, and which get selected out. Over time, the traits that persist are the ones that confer power, not necessarily the ones that make people happiest, or that are most ethical, or that we'd endorse on reflection.

That's where I think it gets important for AI. Advanced AI could be an enormously powerful source of economic and military advantage. If that's true, then actors who are cautious, who slow down, who keep humans in the loop at the expense of efficiency, may find themselves at a competitive disadvantage. And the pressure will push toward delegating more to AI systems, deploying faster, and perhaps trading away values we care about for capability. No single actor needs to want that outcome for it to emerge.

The hopeful side is that these constraints aren't absolute. Selection pressure is strongest when competition is unregulated and the stakes are existential. Humanity has sometimes managed to soften it through cooperation: arms control, international institutions, norms against certain weapons, and periods of hegemonic stability where a dominant power could afford to prioritise things other than raw competitiveness. So one of the central questions for AI governance, in my view, is whether we can build enough coordination to give ourselves room to choose, rather than letting the competitive logic choose for us.

r001.rationale: The response separates actors’ decisions from the competitive selection process that determines which societies persist, and says that process constrains societies’ available choices.

r002.rationale: It describes competition to generate economic surplus and convert it into military power as determining which civilisations persist, linking economic resources to viability.

r003.rationale: It explains that military competition can constrain societies’ choices, but does not say that this pressure can arise after long periods of peace.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about this starts from a fairly simple observation: throughout history, the groups that persisted tended to be the ones that could out-compete their rivals, militarily and economically. And that's not a claim about what's good or what people wanted. It's closer to a selection effect. If you imagine the space of all the possible ways a society could organise itself, all the values it could hold, all the technologies it could choose to adopt or not adopt, only some of those configurations are competitive. The rest tend to get conquered, absorbed, or outgrown.

So you can think of this as a kind of funnel. Individual leaders, individual communities, make choices. Maybe a ruler decides not to adopt firearms because they're dishonourable, or a society decides not to industrialise because it values a particular way of life. Those are genuine choices, and they're often admirable ones. But if a neighbour makes the opposite choice, then over time the neighbour tends to win. And so the civilisations we actually observe persisting are disproportionately the ones that made the competitive choice, regardless of whether that choice was good for the people living in them.

What's interesting to me is how this links the micro and the macro. At the micro level, you have agency. People really are deciding. But at the macro level, the distribution of what survives is shaped by these constraints that no individual chose. I sometimes describe it as the difference between what humanity wants and what humanity does. The Western Roman empire didn't fall because people wanted it to; the agricultural revolution didn't happen because hunter-gatherers thought farming looked like a better life, and most of the evidence suggests it wasn't, at least for a long time. It spread because farming societies could support larger populations and more soldiers.

And the reason I think this matters now, especially with AI, is that you can ask: are we in a world where the competitive pressures are getting stronger or weaker? Because if the pressures are strong, then the range of futures that can actually persist is narrow, and it might not include the futures we'd want. You could imagine a world where the only states or firms that survive are the ones that automate decision-making as aggressively as possible, delegate as much as possible to machines, and move as fast as possible. And that's a world where humans have, in a sense, lost control, not because any one person decided to give it up, but because everyone who kept it fell behind.

The hopeful version of the argument is that this isn't a law of nature. It's a property of the strategic environment. If you can change the environment, through coordination, through institutions, through verification technologies that let rivals trust each other, then you widen the funnel. You expand the set of civilisations that can persist to include ones that are more cautious, more pluralistic, more humane. So the project, as I see it, is partly about understanding how strong these pressures really are, and partly about asking what we'd need to build so that good choices at the individual level don't just get selected away.

r001.rationale: It contrasts individual leaders’ and communities’ choices with higher-level competitive pressures that determine which societies persist.

r002.rationale: It discusses military and economic competition, but does not identify competition for resources as a constraint on viability.

r003.rationale: It explains how military competition can select which societies persist, but does not connect that constraint to competition arising after long periods of peace.

astra-6.text:
Military–economic competition creates a connection between what individuals choose and which societies are able to survive. Individuals might prefer a more peaceful life, more leisure, or institutions that protect things they value. But if those choices leave their society substantially less able to produce wealth or defend itself, it can become vulnerable to societies that organise more effectively for competition.

So there’s a distinction between an arrangement being desirable and it being sustainable in a competitive environment. You can imagine a civilisation that everyone would prefer to live in, but that struggles to persist because it doesn’t generate the resources or military capabilities needed to protect itself. And that pressure can operate without anyone actually wanting the outcome. Each actor can feel compelled to invest more in power because they expect others to do so.

I wouldn’t take that to mean that competition determines everything, or that the most militarised society always wins. Cooperation, trust, and freedom can also be sources of strength. But it does mean we should ask, when imagining a better civilisation: what makes it robust to these competitive pressures? Can we build institutions that constrain competition, so that choices people make for their own flourishing don’t put them at a decisive disadvantage?

r001.rationale: It contrasts individuals’ preferences and choices with the broader competitive pressures that determine whether their society can persist.

r002.rationale: It says societies that generate too few resources or military capabilities can become vulnerable and struggle to persist.

r003.rationale: It describes military competition as a constraint on viable ways of living, but does not mention it arising after long periods of peace.

sol-6.1.text:
Military–economic competition is one of the mechanisms that connects what individuals choose to do with which kinds of societies survive. Individuals can care about all sorts of things — leisure, art, religion, their families. But if the institutions that emerge from those choices leave a society unable to defend itself against competitors, then that society may be conquered, or forced to change its institutions.

So there are two levels of selection here. Within a society, people are pursuing their own goals. Across societies, there’s pressure towards arrangements that generate economic wealth and military power. You don’t need anyone to want that overall outcome for the competitive pressure to push in that direction.

That doesn’t mean there’s one inevitable form of civilisation, or that the most militarily competitive society is the best place to live. It means that persistence imposes a constraint: a civilisation has to be sufficiently competitive, or find some way to make itself secure, to preserve the other things it values. And a central question is how much we can relax that constraint through cooperation, so that competition doesn’t dictate so much of our future.

r001.rationale: It contrasts individuals pursuing their own goals with pressure across societies shaping which arrangements persist.

r002.rationale: It links persistence to economic wealth and military power, but does not identify competition for resources as the constraint.

r003.rationale: It describes military competition as a constraint on survival, but does not address that this constraint can arise after long periods of peace.
